transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2025-11-30
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE); Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE); Sara Liu (HarborCare PM); Diego Ramirez (HarborCare - Lead ML); Priya Nair (HarborCare Sec); Tom (HarborCare Data)

[00:00] Maya: okay hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we have about 45 minutes, we'll run through the quality scorecard, the regressions you flagged and then next steps. quick check, anyone new?
[00:12] Sara: hey Maya, thanks. this is Tom on the data side, just joined to show a couple examples later.
[00:18] Liam: hi all, Liam from Redwood, i'll cover the bench and the runtime asks.
[00:22] Diego: morning, Diego here. we're worried about the uptick in hallucinations post-prompt-tweak.
[00:30] Priya: and i'm Priya, security, i'll just be listening for anything around data retention and KMS.
[00:36] Maya: great. quick recap, last week we rolled prompt v2 which was meant to reduce verbosity; Diego, you sent the report saying the false positive rate on guardrails jumped from 2% to 8%, and the downstream F1 dropped 5 points, is that right?
[00:50] Diego: yep that's the gist. also noticed some switching behavior where the model repeats the disclaimer twice in long threads. might be a prefix caching interaction, maybe kv cash issues? not sure.
[01:06] Liam: kv cash, yeah there's a transcribe there, we mean KV cache, that can interact with prefix trimming if the prompt tokenizer changes. i ran a quick trace on our side and saw that for long convo windows the runtime concatenates cached keys differently for v2 prompts. not necessarily a bug but a behavior change.
[01:28] Sara: can you explain why that would cause more guardrail triggers? the guardrail is mainly a regex plus a semantic rerank, right?
[01:36] Maya: correct, harborcare's guardrail layer has a syntactic filter then a semantic classifier. if the model echoes instructions in a slightly different order the classifier embedding can stray. so even small prompt reorder can push an output across the decision boundary.
[01:52] Diego: here's an example, prompt id 2314: we shortened the priming paragraph and moved the tone note to the top, after that we saw a subset of outputs that hit the phrase "not medical advice" twice and the classifier flagged it as unsafe.
[02:09] Tom: attaching sample 2314A in the sheet, sorry the csv name got truncated in the upload.
[02:18] Maya: no worries. so two parallel tracks: one is immediate guardrail tuning (whitelist the harmless double-disclaimer) and two is investigating model-side behavior and scorecard thresholds.
[02:30] Priya: on the whitelist, are we okay with maintaining manual exceptions? from a compliance point we want auditable rationale.
[02:38] Maya: totally, we recommend storing whitelists as versioned rules in the console so there's an audit trail. we'll include the rationale in the rule metadata.
[02:46] Priya: great. also, KMS question: we're on Azure KMS, will Redwood's private offering support customer-managed keys?
[02:55] Liam: yes, Redwood Private supports customer KMS (Azure/AWS/GCP) and HSM integrations; for hosted we offer envelope encryption with customer-supplied key options for enterprise tiers. i'll send the exact doc.
[03:06] Priya: perfect.
[03:10] Maya: okay back to the scorecard, Diego you had the precision/recall plot?
[03:15] Diego: yes, sharing screen — oh sorry this is the csv export, top row shows baseline (prompt v1) precision 0.87 recall 0.74, v2 precision 0.81 recall 0.72. F1 drop is about 0.04. but the weirdness is the guardrail FP spike.
[03:36] Maya: so we have slightly lower precision, recall similar, but higher FP on the guardrail. it's likely threshold sensitivity. we can do two things: move semantic classifier threshold up (reduce FPs but risk more FNs), or add a small post-rerank that specifically targets the double-disclaimer pattern.
[03:55] Sara: we care more about recall for safety content though, we can't let bad responses slip. so lowering precision for higher recall is ok only if we can avoid noisy guardrail alerts.
[04:08] Maya: understood, we can try targeted exceptions for the false-positive patterns to avoid alert noise while keeping a conservative classifier threshold.
[04:16] Liam: also from infra angle, if you want to keep latency target <200ms p50 on short queries but have a high batching throughput for long ones, Dedicated with a small GPU pool might help. Dedicated also gives predictable cost per token.
[04:33] Diego: what's the delta? we need a rough estimate to include in cost analysis.
[04:38] Liam: ballpark: hosted with batching and quantization — your current mix — is about $0.0018 per 1k tokens for this model; Dedicated could shave 15–25% off that depending on packing and KV cache reuse. i'll produce a more precise spreadsheet with run config.
[04:56] Sara: if we move to Dedicated, do we lose the VPC-on-prem pattern or is that still available?
[05:02] Maya: Dedicated can be in a VPC peering arrangement or we can do Redwood Private for full VPC control/on-prem. Dedicated gives isolation and committed capacity but the control plane is still Redwood-hosted. Private is the full customer-managed control plane.
[05:18] Priya: and audit logs? retention?
[05:21] Maya: we can configure audit log retention per contract; Private allows you to ship logs to your SIEM. Hosted has standard retention windows but enterprise tiers can extend or export.
[05:34] Diego: back to the regressions — can we A/B prompt v1 vs v2 in production traffic sample?
[05:40] Maya: yes that's recommended. run a canary with 20% traffic to v1 and 80% v2 or vice versa depending on risk; Redwood console supports rollout policies and automatic fallback if error rate increases.
[05:52] Liam: for the A/B we'd also recommend capturing intermediate embeddings and the top-k rerank scores to attribute the classifier drift. that helps debug whether the issue is the model surface change or the rerank threshold.
[06:07] Sara: is embedding capture expensive? storage-wise?
[06:11] Liam: it's proportional to sample size; for 10k queries it's trivial. the sensitive bit is retention and PII — if you capture user text you should mask.
[06:21] Tom: quick question, are you able to mask PHI automatically? we have medical examples.
[06:25] Maya: Redwood has optional pre-processing rules to strip or replace PHI tokens; we can show the ruleset.
[06:33] Priya: we require HIPAA-compliant handling; we'll want the Private deployment for production eventually.
[06:39] Maya: understood, that's typical. we can put together a migration path.
[06:43] Diego: looking at some sample failures — here's a case where the model invents a medication dosage. that's the worst type. it's in the examples sheet under failure_09.
[06:52] Maya: ok, those are high severity. for that we should add a hard guardrail to block dosage-like patterns and escalate to human review.
[06:59] Sara: can we tune the classifier to yield an "escalate" label for dosage detection?
[07:04] Liam: yes, you can add a domain-specific binary classifier or a lightweight regex + semantic rule, whichever gives better recall. we'll help you iterate.
[07:13] Diego: on scoring, one edge-case is that our scorer weights precision more than recall currently; we might invert weights for safety content. i will propose a new weighting and share.
[07:24] Maya: great. also want to call out prompt surgery — we saw that moving the tone note to the top changed tokenization boundaries. Diego, can you test moving the tone instruction later in the prompt as an experiment?
[07:36] Diego: yes i can test tone-late vs tone-early. i'll add that to the experiments.
[07:41] Tom: when you talk about tokenization boundaries, are we sure it's tokenizer and not the model's instruction-following?
[07:47] Liam: both can matter. tokenization affects positional attention and the runtime kernel selection; model behavior is also different if the priming text context changes.
[07:58] Maya: ok next let's sketch the immediate remediation plan: 1) whitelist the double-disclaimer pattern (short term), 2) run A/B across 10k samples with embeddings and rerank scores, 3) bench hosted vs dedicated performance, 4) add a dosage hard-guardrail and escalation path.
[08:14] Sara: sound good. can you send the whitelist template so my compliance team can sign off?
[08:18] Maya: yes will send as part of the security package.
[08:20] Priya: please include retention windows and how we can stream logs to Splunk.
[08:25] Liam: noted. also i'll include the perf matrix (p50/p95/p99).
[08:31] Diego: re experiments — do you have guidance on sample stratification? we have chat sessions and API calls, obviously chat has longer context.
[08:39] Maya: stratify by session length and intent. pick 5k short queries (<200 tokens) and 5k long threads (>1k tokens) to cover both.
[08:48] Tom: we'll prepare that export; might take a day to get clean labels.
[08:52] Maya: fine. next, pricing and cost: Sara, what's your internal threshold for per-token cost to be acceptable?
[08:58] Sara: we prefer under $0.002 per 1k tokens for the hosted mix, but if Dedicated reduces ops variability and drops cost by 20% it's worth evaluating.
[09:09] Liam: good note. i'll build a cost sensitivity table in the spreadsheet.
[09:15] Maya: anything else on regressions or scoring?
[09:20] Diego: one more: guardrail false positives are creating alert fatigue for triage. if we can add a confidence bucket that deprioritizes low-severity alerts it will help.
[09:30] Maya: we can add a severity label computed from rerank score + pattern match; low severity can be batched for weekly review.
[09:36] Priya: from compliance perspective we still need to retain all records but we can deprioritize notifications.
[09:41] Maya: yes, retention but notification throttling is fine.
[09:44] Sara: ok let's talk timing: Diego will get failure cases by 12/03, Liam bench by 12/05, Maya send security + whitelist by 12/02, and we'll meet 12/09 for regression triage.
[09:57] Maya: sounds good. anything from the team?
[10:01] Liam: i'll also include a short note on quantization profiles we tested — int8 vs q4 and how they impacted latency.
[10:09] Diego: one operational ask: can Redwood surface token-level attributions in the UI? that would speed debugging.
[10:16] Maya: it's on the roadmap; we can provide export hooks today. we'll capture the feature request.
[10:22] Tom: quick small note — the example csv header had timezone as PST but our events are in UTC, so we had a mismatch.
[10:28] Maya: thanks, call that out in the sheet so we don't misalign.
[10:31] Sara: thanks everyone. recap then i think we're aligned.
[10:36] Maya: recap: Maya send security + whitelist; Diego export failures + test tone placement; Liam run perf bench + cost table; team schedule 12/09 regression triage. we'll attach eval spreadsheet and prompt diffs.
[10:49] Diego: thanks all.
[10:51] Priya: thanks.
[10:53] Maya: thanks team, end.

Notes on transcript: occasional speaker labels were auto-attributed; some technical terms auto-corrected (KV cache -> kv cash) and abbreviations like SOC 2 rendered as SOC two in the raw transcript.
